stages.title: Same amount, different pieces
paragraphs: A fraction describes equal parts of one whole. The denominator counts all equal parts; the numerator counts the parts selected.

Equivalent fractions name the same amount of the SAME whole. Cut each part of a half into two equal pieces: 1 selected part out of 2 becomes 2 selected parts out of 4. The shaded amount stays the same.
Multiply or divide BOTH counts by the same nonzero number. This changes the size and number of pieces, not the amount selected. Compare bars of the same length.

stages.title: See the method
paragraphs: Example: 1/2 = 3/6. Split every half into 3 equal pieces. Numerator: 1 × 3 = 3. Denominator: 2 × 3 = 6.
Example: 2/3 = 8/12. The denominator was multiplied by 4, so multiply the numerator by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8.
Contrast: adding 1 to both counts does NOT preserve the fraction. 1/2 is not 2/3: the same-sized bars show that 2/3 is larger.
Check by simplifying: divide both 8 and 12 by 4 to get 2/3. Never divide a denominator by zero.

stages.title: Try with support
paragraphs: Find the scale factor from the denominator. Apply it to the numerator. Use the bars or a hint if helpful; this is practice.

stages.title: Try on your own
paragraphs: Use a fresh example without looking at a worked answer. You may still ask for support; we will record it as supported practice, never as verified mastery.

stages.title: Fractions in a story
paragraphs: Keep the whole and units the same. Recutting a pizza or changing measurement units must not change the amount.

stages.title: Use the idea another way
paragraphs: Now reason backwards and compare different descriptions. These original tasks explore transfer but have not been educationally validated.

stages.title: Return after a day
paragraphs: Your completed work stays saved. Return after the scheduled day to try different examples without an immediate worked example. These provisional checks cannot verify mastery.

questions.solution: Multiply both counts by 2: 1 × 2 = 2 and 2 × 2 = 4. Thus 1/2 = 2/4.

questions.hint: 3 × 3 = 9. Use the same factor for the numerator.
Compare 4 and 12 to find the multiplier.

questions.prompt: Write 6/10 in simplest form. Enter a fraction.
questions.hint: Find a number greater than 1 that divides both 6 and 10.
questions.solution: Divide numerator and denominator by 2: 6/10 = 3/5. The only common positive factor of 3 and 5 is 1.

questions.prompt: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices. Mira eats 3 slices. If that SAME pizza had been cut into 8 equal slices, how many slices would represent the same amount eaten?
questions.hint: Each original slice is split into 2 equal smaller slices.
questions.solution: The amount eaten is 3/4. Split every slice into 2: 3/4 = 6/8, so 6 smaller slices represent the same amount.

questions.prompt: A ribbon is 2/5 metre long. One metre is divided into 20 equal units. How many of those units make the ribbon?
questions.hint: 5 × 4 = 20. Scale the numerator by 4 as well.
questions.solution: 2/5 metre = 8/20 metre. Each unit is 1/20 metre, so the ribbon contains 8 units.
Divide both numerator and denominator by 2: 10/12 = 5/6. The missing numerator is 5.

questions.prompt: A point is at 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1. Split the SAME interval into 20 equal steps. How many steps from 0 reach the point?
questions.hint: Each quarter contains 5 of the twenty equal steps.
questions.solution: Multiply both counts by 5: 3/4 = 15/20. The point is 15 steps from 0; the interval is still the same whole.
Multiply both counts by 3: 4/7 = 12/21. The missing numerator is 12.

questions.prompt: Write 9/15 in simplest form. Enter a fraction.
questions.hint: Both counts can be divided by 3.
questions.solution: Divide numerator and denominator by 3: 9/15 = 3/5. This is practice, not an educator-verified assessment.
